figures.caption: Figure 1 From frozen backbones to PEFT, and three directions to scale PEFT for brain encoding. (a) The dominant paradigm: a frozen pretrained backbone with readouts trained for brain encoding. The backbone prior is strong, but it is not specialized for brain encoding. (b) We advocate using PEFT to adapt strong pretrained backbones, retaining the powerful prior while allowing flexible neural adaptation. This suggests three complementary scaling directions: Scale up to stronger priors leveraging more capable backbones; Scale down the size of trainable adapters for brain encoding with limited data; and Scale out the number of adapters with different specializations.
Figure 2 One causally masked pass replaces a sliding window. The baseline re-encodes an overlapping window per fMRI timestep; a single pass over the window gives features at every timestep.

Table 1 Main results on CNeuroMod/Algonauts 2025. Validation is on Friends season 6; ID and OOD are the challenge server’s scores on held-out Friends season 7 and OOD movies. Two rows within 0.00077 are not separated by seed variability (App. D). Rows marked † are cited authors’ own numbers quoted from the papers. Our method BrainLoRA achieves a new state of the art.

Figure 4 Modality attribution recovers the canonical topography, and adaptation reweights and mixes the modalities. (a) Contribution to encoding accuracy of the video, audio, and text content, on our LoRA+linear model, left hemisphere (lateral above, medial below). (b) Modality contribution by region. The Shapley terms from the three modalities and a small layout residual sum to the region’s r. (c) Change in modality contribution from the frozen to the adapted model. Audio contribution increases the most, while text falls. (d) Share of the prediction carried from each stimulus modality (left) to the backbone’s output at each modality’s tokens (right), which is the readout’s input. Crossing ribbons are cross-modal mixing within the backbone, which nearly doubles after adaptation.

Figure 5 Scaling out: training a population of adapted models. (a) Training-step time for N rank-16 adapters on a shared backbone: one fused batched gather-matmul vs. N sequential runs. The fused step matches the cost of a single adapter on the same batch (App. C). (b) Ensemble performance vs. ensemble size, averaged over random subsets of the 261 adapted models, which is nearly a straight line in the log-log space (App. G). (c) Performance of 2,000 random 20-model ensembles vs. the performance predicted linearly on two properties of their members: mean single-model accuracy (quality) and mean pairwise residual correlation (diversity). Neither factor predicts ensemble accuracy alone (R2 0.23 and 0.05), but together they predict the performance well (R2=0.97).

Table 3 From MIRAGE’s sliding window to a single causal pass. Friends s06 subject-mean Pearson over four subjects. The sliding-window protocol re-encodes the preceding stimulus at every timestep (∼2,800 forward passes per clip); a single causal pass encodes each clip or window once, and a context lead supplies the preceding stimulus that the first timesteps of a window would otherwise lack. Step time and training cost are for the linear readout. The sliding-window cost is the ∼700 GPU-hours reported by the baseline’s authors, which we reproduced on our hardware (App. C). The frozen MIRAGE head was trained at a 30 s lead and has no longer-lead entries; with LoRA the head was trained at 30 and 60 s, and its re-fit re-solves the per-subject output layer in closed form. Both LoRA column pairs show seed 0. The linear readout has no whole-clip entries because whole-clip encoding is the limit of the context length sweep.

Figure 6 Accuracy within the window. Accuracy against TR position inside the 149 s window for three input designs, scored with the same frozen MIRAGE head on Friends s06 (606 complete interior windows; the band is the s.e.m. over windows for the no-lead configuration). The dashed box marks the first 10 s, where the designs differ. Accuracy here is the per-TR spatial correlation between predicted and measured 1000-parcel patterns, which is defined at a single time point; it is not comparable to the per-parcel headline metric. Without a lead, a window starts 0.110 below its plateau and needs about five TRs to reach it. With a 30 s lead it starts 0.048 below plateau, and with the whole clip 0.051. The first window of each clip is excluded because of a clip-onset transient.

Figure 7 Accuracy against cost. Held-out Friends S7 accuracy against trainable parameters (a) and against endto-end compute including feature extraction (b), both on log scales. Published baselines are squares and our models circles; an N -model ensemble is plotted at N times a member’s cost.

Figure 8 Multi-adapter kernel benchmark. Qwen3-Omni truncated at the feature extraction layer, rank-16 adapters on q/k/v/o, sequence length 128, one sample per adapter, one A800, median of 5 timed steps after 2 warmup steps. (a) One fused batched gather-matmul over N different adapters (blue) matches the same batch through one adapter (grey); running the N jobs one at a time (orange) grows linearly in N . (b) The ratio of the fused pass to the single-adapter batch is 1.00× throughout, up to run-to-run noise of ±0.03.

Table 10 The 261-model pool. Each row is a distinct configuration; members differing only in random seed are grouped, with the seed count given. Entries list only where a member departs from the shipped recipe (Qwen3-Omni backbone, linear readout, feature extraction layer 32, rank 16, 60 s lead, 1,429 steps). Counts sum to 261.

Figure 9 Cross-seed agreement. Mean agreement between adapters over the 15 seeds of the main configuration (105 pairs). (a) At successive levels of the model, from near zero for the weights to near one for the prediction. Levels below the first are cosines between the two seeds’ changes relative to the frozen model, averaged over the audio, video, and text streams. (b) Agreement at every decoder layer, per stream. It rises through the adapted stack, peaks at the feature extraction layer, and declines slowly through the 16 frozen layers above it.

Table 12 The nine omni-modal backbones. Total parameters from each checkpoint’s own index (Qwen3-Omni and Ming are mixture-of-experts, with 3B and 6B active per token); feature extraction layer is chosen per backbone. All arms share the recipe of §5.2: rank-16 LoRA, 60 s context lead, closed-form re-fit, Friends s06 subject-mean.

Table 13 Shifted-target negative control. Friends s06 subject-mean after the closed-form re-fit on aligned training data, one run per configuration. Differences are paired per parcel with a functional-block bootstrap interval; the last column counts the parcels on which the first configuration scores higher.

Figure 10 Performance against the noise ceiling on NNDb. 20 participants, readout re-fitted per participant on the fixed backbone, over the 816 parcels with an estimable ceiling. (a) Subject-mean r per parcel against the corrected noise ceiling (dashed line). (b) Mean percentage of the ceiling per Yeo network.

Table 16 Calibrating a new subject with little data. Validation r of a subject whose fMRI was never used for training the adapter, with its readout fitted on K windows (149 s each) of its own data, shown in minutes. Bold marks the best estimator at each budget. The last row is the gain of the adapted model over the frozen backbone under anchored ridge, which beats it for every subject and draw (20/20) and every NNDb participant (20/20) at every budget. Top: the four 3-subject adapters of Tab. 14, mean over the four held-out subjects and five random draws of the calibration windows; all is the held-out column of Tab. 14, solved on all of that subject’s training data. Bottom: the LoRA+ linear model of Tab. 1 on NNDb, 20 participants, a fixed 7-window test segment and a contiguous calibration run, averaged over placements at the start and end of the film. Its 0min scores therefore differ from Tab. 15, which scores the whole film.

Table 17 Gain from the adapter by region. Validation r with and without LoRA in the same configuration (the frozen arm trains the readout with the same rates and steps), over the n parcels of each region: the seven Yeo networks, then ten ROIs defined from parcel centroids. Arms are paired per parcel; gain intervals are functional-block bootstraps over parcels, and the last column is the gain relative to the frozen score. One run per arm; averaging the LoRA map over 15 seeds leaves both orderings unchanged.

Figure 11 Validation r by region, with and without the adapter. Frozen backbone and the same configuration with LoRA, over the n parcels of each region (Tab. 17); bars show the gain, printed at the right. (a) The seven Yeo networks. (b) Ten coordinate-defined ROIs. One run per configuration, paired per parcel; every gain’s 95% functional-block bootstrap interval excludes zero.

Figure 12 All subsets of the three input streams. Subject-mean Pearson r on the 250 validation windows used for attribution, with absent streams replaced by their training-mean embeddings. The top bar of (a) is the full model (dashed line). (a) Any single stream recovers most of the full score, and removing one costs far less than that stream achieves alone: the streams are largely redundant. (b) Cost of removing each stream, before and after adaptation. The video cost barely changes, the audio cost grows, and the transcript cost falls by more than a third. This removes a stream from a trained model and differs from the no-audio configuration of Tab. 2, which is trained without audio throughout.

Figure 13 Audio contribution by region, before and after adaptation. Subject-mean contribution of the audio stream to encoding accuracy for the frozen and LoRA+ linear models, with episode block-bootstrap intervals; labels give the relative change. Auditory cortex gains least; the gain is largest in regions that relied least on audio before adaptation.
Table 20 Backbone revisions. Hugging Face repository and commit for every backbone in Tab. 12, as loaded by our runs.
